utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The next witness is a judge, and no measures for protection have been requested. It's Mrs. Dijana Ajanovic. I'm sorry. I don't remember who is going to examine this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I will be asking the questions, but my colleague Radovic, if there are any questions left unanswered, he will continue the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will also be asking some questions if there is some time to spare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: She will be examined in chief by Counsel Slokovic-Glumac and, if need be, cross-examined by Counsel Radovic and Pavkovic. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I also propose that this witness be examined as the Defence witness for Vlado Santic, so I think that I should also be conducting the examination-in-chief and not just cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also propose this witness to be examined, so if there are some issues left after my colleague Slokovic-Glumac examines the witness, I will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but then in the form of cross-examination, only as cross-examination. That means that you can't re-examine the witness after the Prosecution's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, this was a joint proposal for this witness to be called. We did that previously. We stated the reasons why we feel that this witness should be brought before the Court. This was a joint motion by my colleague Radovic and myself. For this reason, in fact, we were allowed earlier to call joint witnesses. This is one of the joint witnesses, and I do think that we have the right to examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We don't intend in any way to curtail or restrict your rights, but you should be aware that this will indefinitely prolong our proceedings. On top of that, it may be that the court witness to be called, (redacted), might come only on Friday, so, therefore, we have a lot of time constraints. I hope that you will bear in mind the need to conduct proceedings in the most expeditious way possible. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will take a break at a quarter to eleven for 30 minutes, but meanwhile, we can start. Good morning, Mrs. Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you hear now? Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, and I will call upon Counsel Slokovic-Glumac to start her examination-in-chief, I'm afraid, for five minutes only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Ajanovic. Could you tell us when you were born, where you live, and what you do?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 15th of September, 1953. I still live in Zenica. I worked in various courts for 16 years, and since 1994, I have been an attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are still working as an attorney in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where you were working in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was at the Superior Court in Zenica as a judge. It is a court which has both first instance and second instance jurisdiction, and at that time, it had jurisdiction over 12 municipalities as the appeals court and both as the first instance court. Do I need to go into any more details?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This court also had a criminal department and a civil department?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which department were you employed at that time, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until September 1993, I worked in the civil law department as a judge in the appeals chamber for civil suits, and I was also working in the registry dealing with the registrations of companies, the entering those companies into the court register. As a judge in the civil department, from time to time, I was assigned as a member of a criminal trial chamber, so until the autumn of that year, I sometimes worked in a five-judge chamber dealing with serious criminal offences. From September 1993 on, I have been assigned to the criminal prosecutions department as an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the former system, the qualifications for a judge dealing with criminal cases or carrying out investigations or working on civil lawsuits or in the economic department, the qualifications were the same for all of this?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The requirements were the same for any judge, regardless of the type of cases you were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in 1993, you took over the criminal investigations department, and were you a judge in the court of first instance or the appeals court?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I worked as an investigating judge, but I continued participating in the five-judge chamber when needed. I was not a presiding judge in any of the chambers in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you remember the investigation under official number KI-229/93?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember the investigation, but the reference numbers of the cases were not important to me, so I don't really remember the numbers. But since we are here, I remember that this was an investigation into the crimes committed in the village of Ahmici, in the area of Vitez, the municipality of Vitez, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we take a break now because I would like to have the next part continuously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. A 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Ajanovic, could you please tell the Court who is in charge of an investigation in our system?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the person in charge of an investigation is the investigating judge. There are various kinds of courts: municipal courts, and now there are cantonal courts instead of the higher courts, so that both in the municipal courts and the former high courts, now the cantonal courts, there are investigating judges who are employees of the court and who conduct investigations independently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An investigation may then only be carried out by an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Investigations include examinations of witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can any other person interview a witness, so that the statement can have force of evidence at the main trial, apart from the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness can be interviewed only by an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this procedure of taking witness statements or interviewing witnesses a very formal procedure?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is highly formalised procedure, and it is done in accordance with a special law, the law on criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the record of the interview, does it have force of evidence at the trial conducted pursuant to any indictment?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I need to give a more detailed explanation. Witnesses are interviewed in the course of an investigation, and some other pieces of evidence are also produced. The public prosecutor uses all this evidence to decide at the end of the investigation whether he will or will not file an indictment. In addition to that, the records do have a certain evidentiary value at the trial. In the course of the trial, all the witnesses are examined again, and if a witness does not remember his or her statement given in the course of the investigation, he is confronted with the record in order to remind him of it. If the witness's statement at this stage differs from the statement given before -- so it's not a matter of whether he remembers or not; he is giving now a completely different statement -- he is then asked what is the reason for the difference between this current statement and the previous statement, and if necessary, he is shown his previous statement, which is recorded in this record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the trial, are only those parts of the witness statement departing from or changing the original statement written down, according to the provisions of the law?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the trial, the statement given by the witness at the trial is entered into the record, so not only the parts which are different from his previous statements, but his entire statement. However, if the statement given by the witness at trial conforms completely with his statement given in the course of the investigation, then it needn't be entered into the record, the transcript, again. I have to add something. I did not conclude my answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The records made in the course of the investigation, the records of the interviews conducted with the witnesses, can be used as evidence during the trial in certain cases. It is the case if a witness has died in the meantime, if he has mental illness, if he has developed a mental illness in the meantime, or if he cannot be reached by the court; in other words, if his whereabouts cannot be determined. In cases involving persons who do not have to testify, the spouse of the accused, his or her relatives, up to the third degree -- three times removed, so people who are directly or indirectly related to him, then stepchildren and step-parents, adopted parents and adopted children, then confessors, religious confessors, if they do not attend the trial to which they have been summoned or if they refuse to testify, their records of examination cannot be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This part is not so important to us, but when you said that in certain cases a record given to the investigating judge may be used as evidence without an examination of a witness, and you said that these were records made during an interview and later the witness either dies or becomes mentally ill or cannot be traced, do persons who refuse to testify at the trial -- in other words, are their witness statements used as evidence at the trial?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: If we're dealing with persons who are not bound to testify, their witness statements cannot be used, their records cannot be used. And if a witness refuses to give a statement, if a statement had been given previously in the course of an investigation, the court needs to take the situation into consideration and to bring the statement given during the investigation, bring it into relation with other evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you a very specific question: A witness statement made by a person who refuses to testify at the trial, can it be used?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us whether witnesses giving testimony before an investigating judge are warned that they have to tell the truth and that giving false evidence is a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Every witness, prior to giving his statement, is cautioned that giving false evidence is a criminal offence and that he should not hold back any information, that holding back information is also considered as giving false testimony and that he could be punished with imprisonment for that. It's a usual procedure in courts. Every judge begins the examination of a witness by cautioning the witness in this manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were conducting the investigation, KI-229/93, did you act in the same way? Did you caution every witness?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cautioned every witness. I am used to this procedure. It's impossible for me not to do that. It's really ingrained, this procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued the decision to carry out an investigation? Was it you, or another investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the decision on conducting an investigation was issued by a colleague of mine. Should I tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mensur Hasagic. As far as I remember, he questioned two or three witnesses. After that, I was assigned to this case, and I continued interviewing other witnesses proposed in the request for the initiation of an investigation, which was submitted to the court by the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against whom was the decision on conducting an investigation issued?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember all the names, since this was a case that I dealt with in 1993, and it continued for a while in 1994. When I left the court, I did not take any documents relating to this case with me because this is not usual procedure, to bring any of those documents home. But I do remember the following names: Dario Kordic, Tihofil Blaskic, Ignac Kostroman, Pero Skopljak, Cerkez; I do not recall his first name, Kupreskics; I don't remember whether there were two or three of them on that request. I don't recall the names -- in fact, I do know the names now, but I do not recall the names from before. Santicis, Bralo, Kraljevic, Papic -- well, these are the names that I can remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the file, were there any official police records in the file, any records drawn up by the then-State Security Service, the SDB?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The file contains everything that relates to the case. First of all, from the Ministry of the Interior, a criminal report is filed and is entered into the file together with the supporting material. These are the statements of persons who were questioned preliminarily by the police, and that goes to the public prosecutor, who decided on the basis of those documents that there are grounds for suspicion that persons who are then listed in the request, that they did in fact commit the criminal offence. The public prosecutor then writes and signs a document that is called the request for the institution of an investigation, which is then filed with the court, so that all these documents are contained in one case file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they all bore the same number, the number KI-229/93?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: They had their own individual numbers. The reference numbers of the Ministry of the Interior are different, but they were all in the same case file, KI-229/93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us how you invited or summoned witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was late autumn and winter of 1993/1994. There was a war going on in Bosnia at the time, and of course in Zenica too. The conditions were very hard. We did not have electricity. From time to time our water supply was cut. We did not have fuel for our cars. We had too many refugees in the town and in the surrounding areas, and it was difficult to trace them to determine their address. I issued written summons which were then mailed to those people for whom I had the addresses listed in the request of the prosecutor. For some persons, there was no address listed, and in those cases, I was assigned an official from the Ministry of the Interior whose task it was to go to the areas, to the villages in the area surrounding Zenica, and to ask about the whereabouts of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that person brought the witnesses to you?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: That person was able to find some of them, but in most cases, he left the messages for those persons, telling them that they should come to the court. That person went there on foot. He did not have a car. I asked some of the witnesses who came to tell me where others were and also to relay the message that they should come, so that they did come on the basis of those oral messages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a witness came to the court, did you take their details?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did take their details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their personal details were entered into the official form which has to be filled in when a witness is interviewed?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this record drawn up? Did you tell the witnesses why they were summoned?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give their statements on their own, spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The record was drawn up, first of all, very patiently. Each witness that appeared was first explained why they had been summoned, and they were read the request of the public prosecutor for the investigation. I read out all the names, and I also read the brief explanation of the public prosecutor indicating why this procedure is being done. After that, I asked the witness to tell me everything he or she knew about the events in his or her village in the period from the 15th of April, 1993 and even before that and after that. They told their own story. I interrupted them from time to time in order to dictate for the record their statement. They sat in front of me at a distance of about two metres, and the size of the room in which we were was about 12 square metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they heard you dictating the record?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They told me their story, and I wrote down what they said in pencil. So they were, in fact, dictating it to me. I had to ask them to slow down, to stop in order to be able to write everything down. After that, I dictated that to the person who typed it, to the typist who sat to my left. Each witness was looking at me and listening to me. After I finished dictating, actually, at the end when the record was made, he was given the record to read and to sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the signing of the record follow immediately after the dictation or was there a time gap?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It all happened continuously in that very same room. The witness never left the room until such time when he looked at the record, read the record, and signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present during the signing of the record by the witness?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I gave them the record into their hands and told them, "Please sign."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they sign every page of the record or just the last page?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The records were written on two sheets of A-5 paper, so it was one sheet of paper that was folded up. If the statement was such that it needed to be continued onto the third page -- but if it was only on one page, then the signature was on that page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So each sheet of paper was signed, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also sign the record and the person who typed it out?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all did. That's the usual procedure for all records, not only in criminal proceedings but in civil proceedings too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The signature of the witness means that the witness made the statement. Does it also mean that the witness agrees with the content of the statement?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you remember how many witnesses you interviewed in this case?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I interviewed 20 to 30 witnesses. I really cannot recall exactly. I am, in fact, sorry that I haven't recorded that to take it with me, because I haven't been an employee of the court for five years, and I didn't go to the court to check these things prior to coming here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you complete the investigation in this case?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. In fact, partially, I did, but I do know that the investigation continued afterwards. In late January, I assessed that I could not locate any more witnesses and that I should advise the public prosecutor thereof. At the same time, the witnesses who gave their statements provided information leading to some other names which were not included in the request for the investigation. In accordance with the procedure, the investigating judge, in all cases, must advise the public prosecutor of any such occurrence and leave it to him to decide whether he or she would issue such a request for those new persons and the new crimes. That was the reason why I returned the case to the public prosecutor, so that he could make the decision whether he would expand the investigation to include these other persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of whose statement did that happen; do you remember? 10 (redacted). I think that there were some other statements, but really I cannot remember in such detail. It is in the case file, I wrote a record about all this, and that's why this record exists. That's the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now a general question. Is an investigation mandatory for any criminal offence for which imprisonment of over three or five years is provided for by law? According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, just answer "Yes" or "No," please.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I would now like to have a part of my examination-in-chief in closed session because I need to mention the name of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, do you need a closed session or a private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: A private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Private session. (Private session) .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from September 1993, you were an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we conclude on the basis of what you say about your court experience dealing with various kinds of cases, including criminal cases, that you are a person competent to hear criminal cases? In your opinion, of course.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I passed my bar examination in 1979, and from that time on, I was qualified to work as a judge and as an attorney in all kinds of cases. Of course, work experience is of great assistance to all of us, and of course my colleagues who had been working for a long time dealing with one kind of cases know more about those cases than I do; but on the other hand, there are persons who only start working but know more about those things than some other people who have been working for a long time. It's an individual thing. It is my assessment that I was fully qualified to perform the duties of an investigating judge. As far as being a presiding judge in a court chamber dealing with criminal cases, I did not want to do that job, first of all because I'm a very emotional person, and I did not feel that this job was suitable for me, and that's why I became an attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, I understand that this is a very sensitive matter.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can ask some more questions. Go ahead. But I can say that examining witnesses before the court is a routine matter for a judge such as myself. Before that, I had questioned, interviewed, perhaps three or four thousand witnesses in my previous cases, and it is so simple, really, that there is no reason why I shouldn't able to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In case KI-229/93, you heard, as you have already said, between 20 and 30 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it's closer to 20 than to 30, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would now like to go into private session, because I will mention the name of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: (Open session) Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, at the time the record we're talking about was drawn up on the 17th of December, 1993, what law on criminal proceedings was in force in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a considerable number of laws valid in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been adopted as laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in accordance with the decision/decree issued by the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, published in the Official Gazette, number 2/92. Later on, these laws in the Official Gazette, number 13/92, were confirmed as laws. Over a certain period of time, they were called decree laws, and then they became laws in the full sense of the word again. Among those laws that had been adopted from the previous state was the Law on Criminal Procedure. Some parts of that law had been changed. Those dealing with socialism and Yugoslavia, they were amended to include Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but these are not important points as regards the law itself. What I wanted to ask was, were anybody's rights reduced, particularly, the rights of accused, in comparison with the Law on Criminal Procedure because of the state of war or did the pre-war law fully apply?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure remained the same, but in the course of the war, certain extraordinary legal remedies have been abolished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the investigation procedure remained the same?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the investigation procedure remained the same; detention remained the same. Only the right to an appeal against the indictment was abolished and certain extraordinary legal remedies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the introductory part of the record of the 17th of December, 1993, it says that criminal proceedings are being instituted under Article 141 of the Law on Criminal -- of the Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's genocide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the prescribed sentence?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was five years to death penalty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the old law was still in force?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It included death penalty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the investigation file, when an investigation has been completed and the public prosecutor issues an indictment, what happens to the investigation file? To put it more directly, is the investigation file an integral part of the criminal file or does it remain in the hands of the public prosecutor only for his own information? Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm waiting for the interpretation. The investigation file becomes part of the new file. The investigation file is marked "KI," whereas the main file, the criminal file, has the mark "K." When it enters the trial stage, once the indictment has been issued, the investigation files, together with its folder, becomes a part of the criminal file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the investigation file is ultimately an integral part of the criminal file?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While an investigation procedure is under way, does the investigation file contain every document that comes into the hands of the investigating judge during the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any method of ensuring that all the integral parts of the file are actually in the file or, to be more precise, is there a system which shows that a part of the file is missing, for example? If you don't understand what I'm getting at, I'm referring to the way the pages are numbered and the way the file is put together.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the court, the files are put together in such a way that the last page is, in fact, the first document, and other documents are then placed upon that one and they are all glued together. If somebody were to unglue a page, it would be obvious, but as a rule, it should not be done. It must not be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what mustn't be done is one thing and what is actually done is another. Can you tell me, does every page have a number in the file?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the folder containing the file, on the left-hand side of the interior, there is a list of all the documents, and therein, it is indicated under each number which documents are contained, and each page should be numbered. I have to admit that this is not always done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But in any case, there is a list?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a list. There is also the regulations on the internal operation of the courts which really stipulates all this with great precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The file KI-229/93, do you know where this entire file ended up? This was after you had left the court, of course.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it ended up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you consider that the entire file was delivered to the Prosecutor's office of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I assume so. I never asked anyone about that, but in some unofficial discussions, when I went to the court unofficially, I learned that this file was being translated into English and that the file was being prepared for its final delivery to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The entire file?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that the entire file was submitted here, but I would like to be shown all my records to confirm whether these documents, these records are mine. That may be of no interest to the Court, but I would like to see, to confirm whether these are my documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to this record, in December 1993, with reference to the person named previously, did the Prosecutor of this Court conduct any interview? Don't mention the name, please. The name of the person who signed the record, please don't mention it.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not connected to that person. In the autumn of 1997, a person, a gentleman from the International Tribunal in The Hague was in Zenica. He traced me and talked to me about the way in which I conducted the whole case. He wanted me to explain it all to him. I spoke to him for about 20 minutes and asked him whether this was what he wanted me to tell him. He said that I had understood what he wanted me to say, and then we talked for another couple of hours. He did not show me the record of the person that you're interested in, but this one. Only that one he showed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And the signature?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a copy of the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same one?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this investigator ask about the way in which these records were signed?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I told him that myself. He was interested in that. He did ask questions, but there are no official records about that. He just made some notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the existence of records. I would like to know what he was interested in.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: He wanted to know how I did that, basically the same kind of questions that you're asking, how long did it take me to interview the witness, how I acted towards the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel be asked to make pauses between the questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In our proceedings, at the trial stage, when there is a substantial difference between the statement made during the investigation and during the trial, how does this affect the credibility of the witness in the assessment of the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, is this question relevant? I don't find that it's material to our question. We are not interested in the trial proceedings in Bosnia-Herzegovina. To the best of my knowledge, there was never a trial on this particular issue, on this case. Therefore, what is the relevance of your question? We're interested in what happens here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The relevance, first, is that we now know where the entire investigation file is, which we have not been able to see yet, and it is in the hands of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. This has brought us into the position of not knowing what is contained in the file, and it is only due to the goodwill of the Prosecutor for us to be able to read only what the Prosecutor has decided is exonerating evidence. We are grateful to the Prosecutor for giving us a part of this file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You are speaking at cross purposes. I was objecting to the relevance of your question which was related to the followup of a statement made by a witness before an investigating judge in a trial proper in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think this question is not relevant. As for the file which allegedly - allegedly - because this is a guess by the witness, should be in the hands of the Prosecutor, this is a different issue which you may raise in due time. I wonder whether you could kindly move on, Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have lost my place now, so to speak, my bearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But the question was aimed at getting a reply -- to say that a witness who makes different statements is less credible, but this may or may not be relevant to this Court. I will not go further in this direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Prosecution? Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding the observation made by Counsel Radovic -- oh, I think that Mr. Radovic is now down. Mr. Radovic, are you through with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you finished with your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I am Franck Terrier. I am one of the Prosecutors. I think that you're aware of the fact that I'm going to ask you a number of questions. I'm going to try to be quick. You said earlier, Madam, that after having worked for a long time in civilian occupations, you said that in September 1993 you started working as an investigating judge in a criminal court. Now, is it a deliberate act on your part? I mean, is it an expression of your will? Did you want to become an investigating judge or is this something that was requested from somebody?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the court assigns judges to the tasks in the yearly assignment plan. In wartime conditions, it was not at the beginning of the year but it was sometime in September 1993, he reassigned judges, and he assigned me to this job. It was not what I had wanted, but I knew that he had to do that because the scope of the work in the criminal department was expanding all the time, and he needed more judges. He considered me to be highly competent, and that was the reason why he assigned me to this job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September '93, were you, in Zenica, the only investigating judge or were there more investigating judges?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not the only judge. I have to now make a count. There were four or five other judges. Most of them were men. There was a lady, she was older than I was, and she was the chief of the criminal prosecutions department as the most senior judge at that court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time, if you have any recollection of it, were you in charge of investigating the crimes committed in Ahmici in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I received that case for my procedure sometime in late September. There is a book of assignment in the court. I do not recall the exact date, but there is a book in which I recorded that I received that case for my action. In the course of October, as far as I can remember, I did not summon anyone. I was preparing for this job. It also took some time for the summons to be issued and for the witnesses to receive the summons, especially bearing in mind the fact that it was very hard for the postal service to function. But I also conducted other investigations, not only in this case, but I had some regular cases that I had to deal with. I was also involved partially in the investigation of some other issues related to the work of the Tribunal in The Hague, dealing with cases in which this Tribunal had already issued a judgment. If I may say so, if it is relevant at all, I can even specify the cases, but you probably assume which case it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question regarding your positions at the time, your functions. Did you have to conduct other criminal investigations, apart from the one regarding Ahmici, at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had to. I was assigned to this job, and there was a lot of work at the court. There were also some ordinary criminal offences that had been committed in this area, serious robbery, murder. I conducted investigations into all kinds of criminal offences as they were assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, to have an idea as to your work load of the time, can you tell us approximately how many inquiries you were supposed to conduct at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that it was a war, we did not have a set norm that we had to meet. The requirement was to do one's job properly and honestly. We did not have an obligation to meet a certain number of cases, whereas in the pre-war period, there were such norms set. Everything was done slowly. I have to repeat: In wartime conditions, I was afraid for my own life. I went to work -- while the sirens -- when the sirens indicated that there was an alert, general alert, which meant that I had to be in shelter, I went to work all the same, because in some cases nothing happened, but I went to work all the same. I had to provide some security to all those witnesses, I had to concentrate really hard, I had to be their support, I had to be really strong, to make them believe that there is somebody somewhere in this territory who could make sure that justice is done. I also issued decisions on detention. Everything functioned as it functioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Should we think, then, that at that time, in September '93 up until the end of 1993, that you were a solitary investigator, so to speak? I.e., were you alone in your work, or did you have the possibility to rely on policemen, on other judges, and possibly on the prosecutor or his co-workers? Did you work on your own, or did you have the possibility to rely on other people, including policemen, colleagues, other judges?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contact with police officers. This would not be usual procedure. In my work, since all the judges are on good terms, we're all colleagues, we all work together, we're all at our jobs together, and those who have more experience are always at the disposal of their younger colleagues. So I had both to the left and to the right of my office colleagues with greater experience in this job who spent their entire time in the office with me. I consulted them. Sometimes you wouldn't even know which one of us would have to attend an inside investigation, who would be there to question the next accused. You wouldn't even know which judge would do that. It would be done by that judge who was free at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've explained earlier, madam, that it was upon the request of the prosecutor that you were in charge of investigating on the crimes committed in Ahmici. The prosecutor, on the basis of information that he had at hand, had called that crime genocide. That crime of genocide was provided for in the law enforceable in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Article 141, I even have the book in my purse. I can show you the law and the article itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do believe you, Madam Witness, but just simply --

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here is the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is the definition of the crime of genocide in the law applicable in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when it was committed, according to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Genocide can be committed broadly in two ways. One is persons that order other people to commit murder, grievous bodily harm, or which affect the mental stability of certain persons, with the purpose of exterminating either a national or a religious or a racial group from a certain -- or an ethnic group from a certain area and orders such murders to be committed, persecution, torture in all its forms. That person commits a genocide, as does the person who actually commits all those acts, so that person is also considered to have committed the crime of genocide. I must say, however that, the public prosecutor defined in his request the crime of genocide in its broadest terms, as the broadest type of crime against humanity, which did not mean that had we proceeded to the trial stage in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this qualification would have remained the same. He has the right, after the end of the investigation, to assess on the basis of that material what kind of criminal offence he is dealing with and what kind of indictment he can issue, what can he charge the accused with, whereas the conduct of the investigation does not diminish the value of those statements. They can be used in evidence for other legal qualification of the offence for different criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. You said earlier that the crime of genocide in the law applicable in Bosnia-Herzegovina of the time was punishable by maximum sentence, i.e., the death penalty. As far as you know -- and now I'm no longer talking about the Ahmici events; I'm no longer talking about Ahmici -- but as far as you know, in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the war, were there trials that were conducted for crimes of genocide? And I'm not, again, talking about the crimes in Ahmici or none of the accused, but as far as you know, what is the situation?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not fully informed about everything that is happening in the courts, but I believe that there are no trials going on now for these offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor gives to you a request for an investigation, does he necessarily have to name persons, the people who are affected or concerned, or is it up to him to make the choice of people to be named?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, it's the prosecutor who decides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yourself, as an investigating judge, when you receive a request for an investigation from the prosecutor, do you have to conduct the investigation, or can you refuse to do so when the information, for instance, are considered to be insufficient? Do you have a choice, as an investigating judge, to do that?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: An investigating judge has a council. The council is made up of three judges from the same court, dealing in criminal cases, and if the investigating judge disagrees with a request made by the public prosecutor, he or she has to apply to the council, which will then make a decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence, madam, when you or maybe your predecessor received a request for an investigation from the prosecutor, you considered that request was receivable, that it was valid and that it was well-founded upon the exhibits as filed by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The public prosecutor does not provide evidence. He does not hand over evidence. He provides certain documents from which it is evident that there are reasonable grounds to suspect that the suspect has perpetrated the crime, and the public prosecutor proposes, in his request to the court -- that is, to the investigating judge -- what evidence should be collected or presented. Therefore, it is only before the investigating judge that evidence is presented. Up to that time, it is just in the preparation phase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that there might be a small problem of terminology, and correct me if I'm mistaken in my interpretation of what you said, but it seems that as an investigating judge, that you had examined the request for investigation by the prosecutor, that that request for investigation was based on a number of documents -- I'm not talking about evidence at that stage of the procedure -- and you considered, as an investigating judge, that those documents established reasonable suspicion against the people who were involved to have committed a crime of genocide, and then on that basis, you started your investigation so as to verify or counter the allegations of the prosecutor. Am I right in making this interpretation of things?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are right, but I did not start this investigation. This investigation was started by my colleague, Judge Mensur Hasagic. He was the one who issued a decision that an investigation should be carried out, and it was he who judged that the material handed over by the public prosecutor provided reasonable grounds for an investigation, and there is a list in that decision of all the persons mentioned by the public prosecutor in his request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This colleague whom you are referring to, why didn't he continue his investigation? Why did you have to replace him?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was an internal matter of the court. The president of the court had made the decision that my colleague could not handle all the cases on his own that he was assigned. Sometimes people apply personally. He had already been conducting investigations for a long time, and he wanted to stop doing investigations and to do more in trials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier, madam, that within this investigation, you heard some 20 to 30 witnesses. Did you also do other investigations, for instance, did you go to Ahmici, did you conduct technical visits in houses, things like that? Was it possible at all, given the circumstances and the fact that there was a war?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was absolutely impossible for me to go to Ahmici until the Washington Accords were signed around the 1st of April 1994. There was no way I could have gone to Ahmici because there was gunfire coming from that direction, and shelling. There were two warring sides there, and it was impossible for me to go there. What else did you ask me? I forgot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have answered my question, madam.

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: You asked about sketches?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have fully answered my question. Let me turn to another question: Those 20 to 30 witnesses you've heard, were they all former inhabitants of Ahmici who were victims of the crimes committed in April '93?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were all victims of the crime, but they were not all from Ahmici. A number of them were from other villages. I didn't know, although it's very close to my town, but I didn't know exactly the relative position of all these villages, because I had never had occasion to go there. But I remember they mentioned Grbavica, Gacice, and Nadioci. This has stayed in my memory, the names of these villages. There was a lady who testified to rape who was from Vitez, from the town, and there were people who were not from Ahmici but were from the area of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without referring to one witness in particular, what recollection do you have of those testimonies you've heard regarding the Ahmici crime for the purpose of this investigation? Do you have a feeling that the witnesses appeared to have been very deeply affected, were they experiencing difficult circumstances, did they appear to be very precise, or very imprecise? What is your recollection of how they were?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: The witnesses, when they came before me, it is my impression, tried to be as dignified as possible. They were all deeply affected. All of them had lost either a husband or sons or brothers, fathers. In Ahmici it was mostly men who were killed. It was very difficult and very moving to interview these witnesses. The women would begin their story in a relatively calm manner, but as they continued talking, when they came close in their story to the moment when their husband, son, a brother, is killed, they would then usually break down and start crying. Some of them tried to hold back the tears, to cry as little as possible, but you could see on their faces that they were deeply moved and couldn't conceal their feelings. So at that time, I would stop a little, I would tell them to pause, to take a rest, I would give them a glass of water, offer them a cigarette, some coffee. So the interviews went on slowly. I would wait for them to calm down and then allow them to continue, and that's what the interviews were like. The statements, in most cases, they said that in the evening, on the eve of the 15th of April, the village was quiet, and that they had noticed nothing suspicious, and in the morning, as dawn was breaking, gunfire broke out in the village. There was banging on the doors. People would burst into their houses and kill the male members of their families. They all said that the murderers were some kind of soldiers -- at this moment, I cannot remember exactly what kind of soldiers -- that their faces were painted in various colours, so that most of them were unable to recognise the faces. One group said that they recognised these men and named these persons, and the names they mentioned I entered into the record. It was all the same to me whether the name they mentioned was of this or that person, because I didn't know any of them. I only wrote down or transmitted the names they mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a consequence, madam, the witnesses you saw appeared to be very credible on the whole, trustworthy, and what they were looking for was for justice to be done after the crimes committed in Ahmici; that is the impression which you gathered? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DIJANA AJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, that's how it appeared. On one occasion, the public prosecutor, who was present at a witness interview, after everything she said and the questions I asked, he wanted her to say again who she had recognised. He insisted, saying, "How come you didn't recognise anyone? Who did you recognise?" And she said, "I would like to have recognised someone, I wish I had recognised someone, I wish I knew who these people were." Other people said they saw someone. At the time I was interviewing the witnesses, they were already a bit demoralised. They had been interviewed by the police, then they had come before the court, and the first thing most of them said was, "Why do I have to tell this story again? I've already told it." But when I explained to them that this was a court and that this is the place where their testimony will become evidence, then they understood that, and then they were very happy to tell their stories again in the desire to have those persons punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about another 15 to 20 minutes' worth of questioning, but maybe we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we shall resume tomorrow morning at 9 a.m. I think that (redacted)-- I would like to apologise; I have a lot of trouble pronouncing his name -- I heard that the doctor is ready to come and testify on Thursday, which means that we'll have to get organised. So tomorrow we'll continue with the present witness, and maybe we have now concluded -- we have a list of three witnesses after the witness on Thursday, so maybe we could also hear an expert witness convened by the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic. I think he's the president of the Supreme Court, unless I'm mistaken. Yes, Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time that I heard that (redacted) could be here on Thursday. Although I will limit my examination to a limited range of issues, because, as we know he has already testified before this Court, I will need some time for preparation. I would have to see him at least one day before he testifies, and according to this schedule, that would be impossible. I have to prepare. I cannot come here on Thursday and ask questions of a man I haven't seen in my life, despite the fact that I'm really willing to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, you know, the question is very simple: Either we hear him on Thursday or Friday, or he can't come. So therefore you have to make a choice. In any case, I don't think that you need so much time. To the best of my recollection, it's not a huge issue, the one about which he may be of some relevance. So we could then try to see whether he could be called on Friday, Friday morning, but of course we would then finish with this testimony by Friday at 1.00. Otherwise he will not be able to come back. So you may ponder this question, and then, when we come back tomorrow morning at 9.00, let us know. But as I say, I know he is available on Thursday morning. That's why I was suggesting that we should organise our proceedings in such way as to start on Thursday morning with him. He will be here on Wednesday, I understand, tomorrow. And then -- you know, in the afternoon, we are all free, in inverted commas; namely, we work on other matters. You could probably, tomorrow afternoon, if he is around, so Wednesday afternoon and possibly Thursday afternoon. Is that fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it's necessary for him to be examined this week. Maybe his testimony could be postponed until the witnesses in the Defence for Vladimir Santic are here. No? Well, I will abide by your decision, but please allow me some reasonable time for my preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. All right. So therefore we can adjourn now until tomorrow at 9, and we will go -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to advise the Court that the witnesses in the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic called according to the list presented to the Court are all here in The Hague except for the one who has fallen ill, and we are prepared to start the examination of two or three of them. Our first witness would be Vjenceslav Ilic, the president of the Supreme Court, and then we can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, I very much hope that we can start with Mr. Ilic tomorrow after the present witness, and I very much hope that his testimony will be brief, because as I warned you, we will not go into legal technicalities about the notion of persecution in the Yugoslav law, because it is for this Court to decide what is meant by "persecution." We don't want to have a big picture of the legal technicalities of the legal system in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I hope that you will ask questions brief and material to our case. In this case, if this is so, we could even tomorrow move on to the second witness you intended to call. Thank you so much. We adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1:10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of May, 1999, at 9:00 a.m.
